claim: Netarsudil decreased glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension in patients whose intraocular pressures were poorly controlled by standard medications.
source: We report that netarsudil, a rho-kinase inhibitor, decreased glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension in patients whose intraocular pressures were poorly controlled by standard medications.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the study, supported by patient data presented in the results section.

claim: Netarsudil both prevented and reduced intraocular pressure elevation in a mouse model of glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension.
source: Mechanistic studies in our established mouse model of glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension show that netarsudil both prevented and reduced intraocular pressure elevation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from mouse studies shown in Figure 2.

claim: Netarsudil attenuated characteristic steroid-induced pathologies as assessed by quantification of outflow function and tissue stiffness.
source: Further, netarsudil attenuated characteristic steroid-induced pathologies as assessed by quantification of outflow function and tissue stiffness, and morphological and immunohistochemical indicators of tissue fibrosis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by multiple measurements including outflow facility (Figure 2), tissue stiffness (Figure 3), and morphological analysis (Figures 4-5).

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors act directly on conventional outflow cells to prevent or attenuate fibrotic disease processes in glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension in an immune-privileged environment.
source: Thus, rho-kinase inhibitors act directly on conventional outflow cells to prevent or attenuate fibrotic disease processes in glucocorticoid-induced ocular hypertension in an immune-privileged environment.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by the mechanistic studies in the mouse model and discussion of the eye's immune-privileged status.

claim: 90% of people with primary open-angle glaucoma develop ocular hypertension after glucocorticoid treatment.
source: Interestingly, 90% of people with primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG), the most common type of glaucoma, develop OHT after GC treatment (Becker, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Becker, 1965.

claim: The rate of ocular hypertension after glucocorticoid treatment in people with primary open-angle glaucoma is more than double the rate of the general population.
source: This is more than double the rate of the general population, likely because GCs increase extracellular matrix (ECM) material, cell contractility, and stiffness in an already dysfunctional conventional outflow pathway (Johnson et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 1998), as is found in POAG (Rönkkö et al., 2007; Tamm and Fuchshofer, 2007).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Glucocorticoids increase extracellular matrix material, cell contractility, and stiffness in the conventional outflow pathway.
source: This is more than double the rate of the general population, likely because GCs increase extracellular matrix (ECM) material, cell contractility, and stiffness in an already dysfunctional conventional outflow pathway (Johnson et al., 1997; Zhou et al., 1998), as is found in POAG (Rönkkö et al., 2007; Tamm and Fuchshofer, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Johnson et al., 1997 and Zhou et al., 1998.

claim: The conventional outflow pathway drains the majority of the aqueous humor.
source: The conventional outflow pathway drains the majority of the aqueous humor, and its hydrodynamic resistance is the primary determinant and homeostatic regulator of IOP (Tamm, 2009).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Tamm, 2009.

claim: The hydrodynamic resistance of the conventional outflow pathway is the primary determinant and homeostatic regulator of intraocular pressure.
source: The conventional outflow pathway drains the majority of the aqueous humor, and its hydrodynamic resistance is the primary determinant and homeostatic regulator of IOP (Tamm, 2009).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Tamm, 2009.

claim: Pro-fibrotic changes in the conventional outflow pathway frequently lead to significantly elevated intraocular pressures.
source: Thus, pro-fibrotic changes in this outflow pathway, such as occurring with GC treatment, frequently lead to significantly elevated IOPs (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2018.

claim: Rho-associated protein kinase is a major cytoskeletal regulator in health and disease.
source: Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) is a major cytoskeletal regulator in health and disease.
evidence: This is a general statement about ROCK supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in fibrotic kidney disease.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Musso et al., 2017.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marinković et al., 2013 and Knipe et al., 2015.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in cardiac fibrosis.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Olson, 2008 and Haudek et al., 2009.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crespi et al., 2020.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in vitreoretinal disease.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamaguchi et al., 2017.

claim: ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in lens capsule opacity.
source: Indeed, ROCK mediates pro-fibrotic processes in many tissues and pathological conditions, including fibrotic kidney disease (Musso et al., 2017), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Marinković et al., 2013; Knipe et al., 2015), cardiac fibrosis (Olson, 2008; Haudek et al., 2009), liver fibrosis, intestinal fibrotic strictures associated with Crohn's disease (Crespi et al., 2020), vitreoretinal disease (Yamaguchi et al., 2017), and lens capsule opacity (Korol et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Korol et al., 2016.

claim: The eye has immune-privileged status.
source: Mechanistic studies evaluating anti-fibrotic activity of ROCKi in the eye are particularly interesting in view of the eye's immune-privileged status (Streilein, 2003), which minimizes the role of macrophages and monocytes as compared to other organ systems.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Streilein, 2003.

claim: The eye's immune-privileged status minimizes the role of macrophages and monocytes as compared to other organ systems.
source: Mechanistic studies evaluating anti-fibrotic activity of ROCKi in the eye are particularly interesting in view of the eye's immune-privileged status (Streilein, 2003), which minimizes the role of macrophages and monocytes as compared to other organ systems.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Streilein, 2003.

claim: Ocular hypertension in glaucoma patients is the only approved indication for rho-kinase inhibitors in humans.
source: In fact, OHT in glaucoma patients is the only approved indication for ROCKi in humans thus far (Roskoski, 2020).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Roskoski, 2020.

claim: Ripasudil and netarsudil have been approved for clinical use to treat ocular hypertension in glaucoma patients.
source: Specifically, two ROCKi, ripasudil and netarsudil (NT), have been approved for clinical use to treat OHT in glaucoma patients because of their safety profile and IOP-lowering ability and ultimately their unique mechanism of action (Garnock-Jones, 2014; Isobe et al., 2014; Tanihara et al., 2015; Kopczynski and Heah, 2018; Serle et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors are the only available glaucoma drug class that directly targets and improves conventional outflow function.
source: Therefore, ROCKi are the only available glaucoma drug class that directly targets and improves conventional outflow function (Schehlein and Robin, 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Schehlein and Robin, 2019.

claim: The first patient cohort included 21 eyes of 19 patients with a mean age of 66.8 years.
source: Our search identified 21 eyes of 19 patients (mean age 66.8 years), treated with GCs for a variety of ocular conditions and who demonstrated OHT secondary to GC treatment (Table 1, cohort 1).
evidence: This is a description of the patient cohort directly stated in the results section.

claim: Steroid-responsive patients in cohort 1 were initially treated with aqueous humor suppressants.
source: In accordance with current standard of treatment, these steroid-responsive patients were initially treated with aqueous humor suppressants (e.g., carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and/or adrenergics, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the treatment history of cohort 1.

claim: Prostaglandin analogues were typically used as second-line therapies in cohort 1 due to concerns about possible pro-inflammatory effects.
source: We note that prostaglandin analogues were typically used as second-line therapies (or not at all) in this patient cohort, due to concerns about the possible pro-inflammatory effects of these agents (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the treatment approach for cohort 1.

claim: Patients in cohort 1 presented with an average IOP of 24.3 ± 6.6 mmHg before netarsudil treatment.
source: Unfortunately, these first- and second-line medications did not adequately control IOP in these patients, who presented with an average IOP of 24.3 ± 6.6 mmHg before NT treatment (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: Netarsudil treatment resulted in a clinically significant lowering of IOP in all patients in cohort 1 within 1 month, with an average IOP decrease of 7.9 mmHg (p=1.2×10−7).
source: Thus, NT treatment was initiated, resulting in a clinically significant lowering of IOP in all patients within 1 month, presenting an average IOP decrease of 7.9 mmHg (p=1.2×10−7, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1A with statistical significance.

claim: IOP in cohort 1 was reduced to an average of 16.4 ± 4.9 mmHg after netarsudil treatment, which is within the normal range.
source: In this cohort, IOP was reduced to an average of 16.4 ± 4.9 mmHg, which is within the normal range.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: None of the patients in cohort 1 were tapered from their steroid during the first month of netarsudil treatment.
source: It is important to note that none of the patients were 'tapered' from their steroid during the first month of treatment, and thus the observed IOP lowering cannot be due to a removal of steroid.
evidence: This is stated in the results section to clarify that IOP lowering was due to netarsudil, not steroid withdrawal.

claim: The observed IOP lowering in cohort 1 cannot be due to removal of steroid.
source: It is important to note that none of the patients were 'tapered' from their steroid during the first month of treatment, and thus the observed IOP lowering cannot be due to a removal of steroid.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results section based on the fact that steroids were not tapered.

claim: Cohort 2 included 11 eyes from eight patients with an average age of 58.4 years.
source: We identified 11 eyes from eight patients, with an average age of 58.4 years (Table 1, Cohort 2).
evidence: This is a description of the patient cohort directly stated in the results section.

claim: The IOP in cohort 2 prior to netarsudil treatment was 26.5 ± 7.7 mmHg.
source: The IOP in these eyes prior to NT treatment was similar to the first cohort at 26.5 ± 7.7 mmHg (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: Netarsudil significantly lowered IOP in cohort 2 by an average of 7.0 mmHg (p=0.0003).
source: As well, NT significantly lowered IOP in this second cohort by an average of 7.0 mmHg (p=0.0003, Figure 1B), leading to an IOP of 19.5 ± 5.8 mmHg (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section and shown in Figure 1B with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil significantly lowers IOP in steroid glaucoma patients who were refractory to conventional anti-ocular hypertensive medications.
source: We conclude that NT significantly lowers IOP in steroid glaucoma patients who were refractory to conventional anti-ocular hypertensive medications.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on data from both patient cohorts.

claim: Daily treatment with netarsudil significantly decreases IOP in naïve mouse eyes by improving conventional outflow function.
source: It is known that daily treatment with NT significantly decreases IOP in naïve mouse eyes by improving conventional outflow function (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2016.

claim: Baseline IOPs in both netarsudil and placebo groups in the prevention study were similar (19.4 ± 0.4 and 19.6 ± 1.1 mmHg, respectively, p=0.60).
source: Baseline IOPs in both NT and PL groups were similar (19.4 ± 0.4 and 19.6 ± 1.1 mmHg, respectively, p=0.60).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: One day after netarsudil or placebo treatment, but before dexamethasone treatment, IOP was 20.1 ± 0.9 mmHg in placebo-treated eyes and significantly lower (16.1 ± 1.4 mmHg) in netarsudil-treated eyes (p=0.0009).
source: One day after NT or PL treatment, but before DEX treatment, IOP was 20.1 ± 0.9 mmHg in PL-treated eyes and significantly lower (16.1 ± 1.4 mmHg) in NT-treated eyes (p=0.0009, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2A with statistical significance.

claim: Average IOP elevation in placebo-treated eyes in the prevention study was 5.94 ± 0.57 mmHg over 4 weeks.
source: IOPs were followed for 4 weeks, and average IOP elevation in PL-treated eyes was 5.94 ± 0.57 mmHg, while IOP in NT-treated eyes was significantly lower than IOP in PL eyes (p<0.0001, Figure 2B), returning close to baseline levels (average IOP elevation compared to baseline of 0.23 ± 0.45 mmHg, p=0.71).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: IOP in netarsudil-treated eyes in the prevention study was significantly lower than IOP in placebo eyes (p<0.0001).
source: IOPs were followed for 4 weeks, and average IOP elevation in PL-treated eyes was 5.94 ± 0.57 mmHg, while IOP in NT-treated eyes was significantly lower than IOP in PL eyes (p<0.0001, Figure 2B), returning close to baseline levels (average IOP elevation compared to baseline of 0.23 ± 0.45 mmHg, p=0.71).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B with statistical significance.

claim: IOP in netarsudil-treated eyes in the prevention study returned close to baseline levels with an average IOP elevation compared to baseline of 0.23 ± 0.45 mmHg (p=0.71).
source: IOPs were followed for 4 weeks, and average IOP elevation in PL-treated eyes was 5.94 ± 0.57 mmHg, while IOP in NT-treated eyes was significantly lower than IOP in PL eyes (p<0.0001, Figure 2B), returning close to baseline levels (average IOP elevation compared to baseline of 0.23 ± 0.45 mmHg, p=0.71).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Outflow facility was 84% greater in netarsudil eyes compared to placebo in the prevention study (4.87 ± 1.09 vs. 2.64 ± 0.44 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.08).
source: Outflow facility, the primary determinant of IOP, was 84% greater in NT eyes compared to PL (4.87 ± 1.09 vs. 2.64 ± 0.44 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.08, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Long-term treatment with netarsudil appeared to impact outflow facility in both treated and contralateral eyes.
source: Long-term treatment with NT appeared to impact outflow facility in both treated and contralateral eyes (4.87 vs. 4.39 nl/min/mmHg, respectively), likely due to contralateral effects as observed previously with DEX (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The baseline IOPs before dexamethasone treatment in both netarsudil and placebo groups in the reversal study were similar (18.5 ± 1.76 vs. 19.2 ± 1.28 mmHg, respectively, p=0.21).
source: The baseline IOPs before DEX treatment in both NT and PL groups were similar (18.5 ± 1.76 vs. 19.2 ± 1.28 mmHg, respectively, p=0.21).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: After 3 weeks of dexamethasone-nanoparticle treatment, average IOP elevation compared to baseline in placebo and netarsudil cohorts was similar (6.77 ± 0.67 vs. 7.74 ± 0.384 mmHg, respectively, p=0.45).
source: After 3 weeks of DEX-NP treatment, average IOP elevation (days 3–21) compared to baseline in PL and NT cohorts was similar (6.77 ± 0.67 vs. 7.74 ± 0.384 mmHg, respectively, p=0.45, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Commencement of netarsudil treatment resulted in rapid IOP lowering within 1 day.
source: Commencement of NT treatment resulted in rapid IOP lowering (within 1 day) followed by a continued decrease.
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section.

claim: After 4 days of netarsudil treatment in the reversal study, the change in IOP from baseline in placebo-treated eyes was 8.19 ± 0.46 vs. 2.69 ± 0.47 mmHg for netarsudil-treated eyes (p<10−4).
source: After 4 days of treatment, the change in IOP from baseline in PL-treated eyes was 8.19 ± 0.46 vs. 2.69 ± 0.47 mmHg for NT-treated eyes (p<10−4).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil almost completely reversed steroid-induced ocular hypertension, returning IOP to near baseline levels (18.5 ± 1.76 vs. 21.4 ± 1.30 mmHg).
source: In fact, NT almost completely reversed steroid-induced OHT, returning IOP to near baseline levels (18.5 ± 1.76 vs. 21.4 ± 1.30 mmHg).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: Netarsudil increased outflow facility by 33% compared to placebo in the reversal study (5.18 ± 0.57 vs. 3.48 ± 0.51 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.038).
source: NT increased outflow facility by 33% compared to PL (5.18 ± 0.57 vs. 3.48 ± 0.51 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.038, Figure 2F) and increased outflow by 37% compared to contralateral eyes (3.27 ± 0.49 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.025).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 2F with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil increased outflow facility by 37% compared to contralateral eyes in the reversal study (p=0.025).
source: NT increased outflow facility by 33% compared to PL (5.18 ± 0.57 vs. 3.48 ± 0.51 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.038, Figure 2F) and increased outflow by 37% compared to contralateral eyes (3.27 ± 0.49 nl/min/mmHg, p=0.025).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section with statistical significance.

claim: Measured facility differences can mathematically account for 93–102% of the observed IOP differences between netarsudil- and placebo-treated eyes, assuming no effect of netarsudil on aqueous inflow rate.
source: Assuming no effect of NT on aqueous inflow rate, these measured facility differences can mathematically account for 93–102% of the observed IOP differences between NT- and PL-treated eyes, both here and in the prevention study.
evidence: This is a calculation stated in the results section based on measured facility and IOP data.

claim: If a 10–15% reduction of aqueous inflow is accounted for, the measured facility differences account for 85–95% of the observed IOP changes.
source: If a 10–15% reduction of aqueous inflow is accounted for, the measured facility differences account for 85–95% of the observed IOP changes.
evidence: This is a calculation stated in the results section based on measured facility and IOP data with an assumption about inflow reduction.

claim: Netarsudil's IOP-lowering effect in the steroid glaucoma model can be largely explained by increased outflow facility.
source: We conclude that NT's IOP-lowering effect in this steroid glaucoma model can be largely explained by increased outflow facility.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the facility and IOP measurements.

claim: Mechanical stiffness of the trabecular meshwork was shown to be increased by glucocorticoid treatment, negatively correlating with outflow facility.
source: Mechanical stiffness of the TM, a key tissue in the conventional outflow pathway, was shown to be increased by GC treatment, negatively correlating with outflow facility (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Glucocorticoid treatment decreased the tendency of the Schlemm's canal lumen to collapse at elevated IOPs.
source: We also previously showed that GC treatment decreased the tendency of the Schlemm's canal (SC) lumen to collapse at elevated IOPs (Li et al., 2019), an effect that appeared to be mediated by changes in TM stiffness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The SC luminal cross-sectional areas differed significantly between netarsudil- and placebo-treated groups at each pressure level (p=0.0024).
source: In fact, the SC luminal cross-sectional areas differed significantly between NT- and PL-treated groups at each pressure level (p=0.0024, Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3 with statistical significance.

claim: Inverse finite element modeling deduced TM tissue stiffness values of 22 kPa in the netarsudil-treated group vs. 61 kPa in the placebo-treated group.
source: We deduced TM tissue stiffness values of 22 kPa in the NT-treated group vs. 61 kPa in the PL-treated group (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The TM stiffness in placebo-treated eyes (61 kPa) is consistent with the TM stiffness previously measured in dexamethasone-nanoparticle treated eyes of 69 kPa.
source: The latter value is consistent with the TM stiffness we previously measured in DEX-NP treated eyes of 69 kPa (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The TM stiffness estimated in netarsudil-treated eyes (22 kPa) was close to the value of 29 kPa previously determined in naïve eyes.
source: Notably, the TM stiffness we estimated in NT-treated eyes was close to the value of 29 kPa that we previously determined in naïve eyes (Li et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Netarsudil returns TM stiffness to near control levels after only 4 days of administration in eyes made hypertensive by long-term glucocorticoid administration.
source: Thus, it appears that NT returns TM stiffness to near control levels after only 4 days of administration in eyes made hypertensive by long-term GC administration.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the iFEM stiffness measurements.

claim: Netarsudil significantly reduced TM tissue stiffness by 23% compared to contralateral eyes (1.54 ± 0.19 vs. 2.00 ± 0.13 kPa, p=0.007) as measured by atomic force microscopy.
source: Using the reversal treatment protocol, we observed that NT significantly reduced TM tissue stiffness by 23% compared to contralateral eyes (1.54 ± 0.19 vs. 2.00 ± 0.13 kPa, p=0.007, Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 3H with statistical significance.

claim: Placebo did not affect TM tissue stiffness compared to contralateral eyes (1.39 ± 0.12 vs. 1.73 ± 0.20 kPa, p=0.39).
source: In contrast, PL did not affect TM tissue stiffness compared to contralateral eyes (1.39 ± 0.12 vs. 1.73 ± 0.20 kPa, p=0.39).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section.

claim: No gross morphological changes were observed in conventional outflow tissues in netarsudil- vs. placebo-treated steroid-induced ocular hypertension eyes at the light microscopic level.
source: At the light microscopic level, we observed no gross morphological changes in conventional outflow tissues in NT- vs. PL-treated steroid-induced OHT eyes (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Netarsudil treatment reduced the expression of alpha smooth muscle actin in the trabecular meshwork.
source: In contrast, we observed that NT treatment reduced the expression of alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA; Figure 4H vs. 4I) and fibronectin (FN; Figure 4E vs. 4F), two fibrotic indicators known to be elevated in conventional outflow tissues after GC treatment.
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Netarsudil treatment reduced the expression of fibronectin in the trabecular meshwork.
source: In contrast, we observed that NT treatment reduced the expression of alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA; Figure 4H vs. 4I) and fibronectin (FN; Figure 4E vs. 4F), two fibrotic indicators known to be elevated in conventional outflow tissues after GC treatment.
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: Alpha smooth muscle actin and fibronectin are fibrotic indicators known to be elevated in conventional outflow tissues after glucocorticoid treatment.
source: In contrast, we observed that NT treatment reduced the expression of alpha smooth muscle actin (αSMA; Figure 4H vs. 4I) and fibronectin (FN; Figure 4E vs. 4F), two fibrotic indicators known to be elevated in conventional outflow tissues after GC treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as established knowledge.

claim: Netarsudil treatment significantly reduced alpha smooth muscle actin expression (p=0.037).
source: Results indicate that NT treatment significantly reduced both αSMA (4K, p=0.037) and FN protein expression (4J, p=0.007).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4K with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil treatment significantly reduced fibronectin protein expression (p=0.007).
source: Results indicate that NT treatment significantly reduced both αSMA (4K, p=0.037) and FN protein expression (4J, p=0.007).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 4J with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil-mediated down-regulation led to alpha smooth muscle actin and fibronectin levels similar to those observed in eyes treated with phosphate buffered saline-loaded nanoparticles and naïve eyes.
source: In fact, NT-mediated down-regulation led to αSMA and FN levels similar to those observed previously in eyes treated with phosphate buffered saline (PBS)-loaded (sham) NPs (Li et al., 2019) and naïve eyes (4D and 4G).
evidence: This comparison is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: Netarsudil treatment resulted in a significant reduction in the amount and density of basement membrane materials underlying the inner wall of Schlemm's canal.
source: When examined at the electron microscopic level, we observed two major effects of NT treatment on steroid-induced OHT eyes (Figure 5). The first was a significant reduction in the amount and density of basement membrane materials (BMM) underlying the inner wall of SC.
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Netarsudil treatment resulted in an apparent increase in the number of 'open spaces' in the trabecular meshwork, particularly in the juxtacanalicular region.
source: The second was an apparent increase in the number of 'open spaces' in the TM of NT-treated eyes, particularly in the juxtacanalicular (JCT) region.
evidence: This observation is stated in the results section.

claim: Semi-quantitative scoring confirmed observational impressions of netarsudil treatment on extracellular matrix in the juxtacanalicular region (p=0.02).
source: These two changes were scored on a semi-quantitative scale, confirming observational impressions of NT treatment (Figure 5F, p=0.02).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5F with statistical significance.

claim: Length of basement membrane materials underlying Schlemm's canal was significantly increased in mice after dexamethasone treatment (p<0.001).
source: Similar to results reported in Overby et al., we found that length of BMM underlying SC was significantly increased in mice after DEX treatment (Figure 5G, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance.

claim: There were significant differences in basement membrane material measurements between placebo- and netarsudil-treated eyes (p=0.001).
source: Most importantly, these data confirm significant differences between PL- and NT-treated eyes (Figure 5G, p=0.001), whereby NT appears to partially restore the ultrastructure of the subendothelial region.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement stated in the results section and shown in Figure 5G with statistical significance.

claim: Netarsudil appears to partially restore the ultrastructure of the subendothelial region.
source: Most importantly, these data confirm significant differences between PL- and NT-treated eyes (Figure 5G, p=0.001), whereby NT appears to partially restore the ultrastructure of the subendothelial region.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results section based on the basement membrane material measurements.

claim: Netarsudil effectively decreased steroid-induced ocular hypertension in two different cohorts of patients who were refractory to standard glaucoma medications.
source: The major finding of the current study was that NT effectively decreased steroid-induced OHT in two different cohorts of patients who were refractory to standard glaucoma medications.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the patient data presented in the results.

claim: Netarsudil decreased long-term steroid-induced ocular hypertension in mice.
source: As in patients, NT decreased long-term steroid-induced OHT in mice and also prevented the onset of steroid-induced OHT.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the mouse data presented in the results.

claim: Netarsudil prevented the onset of steroid-induced ocular hypertension in mice.
source: As in patients, NT decreased long-term steroid-induced OHT in mice and also prevented the onset of steroid-induced OHT.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the mouse data presented in the results.

claim: Netarsudil-mediated rescue of ocular hypertension in mice was accompanied by restoration of normal outflow facility and conventional outflow tissue stiffness.
source: NT-mediated rescue of OHT in mice was accompanied by restoration of normal outflow facility and conventional outflow tissue stiffness, as well as significant morphological alterations in the TM.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the mouse data presented in the results.

claim: Netarsudil-mediated rescue of ocular hypertension in mice was accompanied by significant morphological alterations in the trabecular meshwork.
source: NT-mediated rescue of OHT in mice was accompanied by restoration of normal outflow facility and conventional outflow tissue stiffness, as well as significant morphological alterations in the TM.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the discussion based on the mouse data presented in the results.

claim: Calculations suggest that the IOP effect seen in netarsudil-treated mice was mostly or entirely explainable by changes in outflow facility.
source: Calculations suggest that the IOP effect seen in NT-treated mice was mostly or entirely explainable by changes in outflow facility, which together with our direct and indirect measurements of TM stiffness implicate the TM as the tissue mediating the effects of NT on IOP.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on calculations presented in the results.

claim: The trabecular meshwork is the tissue mediating the effects of netarsudil on intraocular pressure.
source: Calculations suggest that the IOP effect seen in NT-treated mice was mostly or entirely explainable by changes in outflow facility, which together with our direct and indirect measurements of TM stiffness implicate the TM as the tissue mediating the effects of NT on IOP.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on calculations and stiffness measurements.

claim: This is the first demonstration of prevention and rescue from steroid-induced ocular hypertension by a trabecular meshwork-active FDA-approved glaucoma medication.
source: Thus, this is the first demonstration of prevention and rescue from steroid-induced OHT by a 'TM-active' FDA-approved glaucoma medication and suggests that ROCKi compounds have effective anti-fibrotic activity in the TM.
evidence: This is a claim of novelty stated in the discussion.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitor compounds have effective anti-fibrotic activity in the trabecular meshwork.
source: Thus, this is the first demonstration of prevention and rescue from steroid-induced OHT by a 'TM-active' FDA-approved glaucoma medication and suggests that ROCKi compounds have effective anti-fibrotic activity in the TM.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: A rho-kinase inhibitor lowered IOP in a transgenic mouse locally overexpressing connective tissue growth factor.
source: Our results extend findings from an earlier report showing that a ROCKi lowered IOP in a transgenic mouse locally overexpressing connective tissue growth factor (CTGF) (Junglas et al., 2012), to a clinically relevant disease context by demonstrating NT activity in the conventional outflow pathway.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Junglas et al., 2012.

claim: Two significant phenotypic changes were observed in netarsudil-treated eyes with ocular hypertension: rapid reversal of IOP elevation within 1–2 days.
source: Importantly, two significant phenotypic changes were observed in NT-treated eyes with OHT. The first was a rapid reversal of IOP elevation (within 1–2 days).
evidence: This observation is stated in the discussion based on the results.

claim: Two significant phenotypic changes were observed in netarsudil-treated eyes with ocular hypertension: a significant decrease in accumulated extracellular matrix materials.
source: The second was a significant decrease in accumulated ECM materials, namely FN and basal lamina material underlying the inner wall of SC.
evidence: This observation is stated in the discussion based on the results.

claim: Both cellular contractility changes and extracellular matrix changes likely contribute to the observed decrease of trabecular meshwork tissue stiffness by netarsudil.
source: Both cellular contractility changes and ECM changes likely contribute to the observed decrease of TM tissue stiffness by NT.
evidence: This is an interpretation stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: The observed changes in extracellular matrix composition and amount may be due to netarsudil-mediated opening of flow pathways and consequential removal of extracellular matrix.
source: In addition to NT-mediated changes in ECM turnover, the observed changes in ECM composition and amount may also be due to NT-mediated opening of flow pathways and consequential removal of ECM.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation stated in the discussion.

claim: Alterations in the biomechanical properties (i.e., stiffening) of the trabecular meshwork are observed in glaucomatous human donor eyes.
source: For example, alterations in the biomechanical properties (i.e., stiffening) of the TM are observed in glaucomatous human donor eyes, which were hypothesized to be associated with dysregulation of the ECM (Lütjen-Drecoll et al., 1986; Yue, 1996; Tamm and Fuchshofer, 2007; Keller et al., 2009; Tektas and Lütjen-Drecoll, 2009; Last et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Trabecular meshwork stiffening and elevated IOP were observed in animal models of steroid-induced ocular hypertension.
source: TM stiffening and elevated IOP were also observed in animal models of steroid-induced OHT (Raghunathan et al., 2015; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raghunathan et al., 2015 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: Trabecular meshwork tissue stiffness is associated with increased outflow resistance in steroid-induced ocular hypertension mouse eyes.
source: In a recent study, we showed that TM tissue stiffness is associated with increased outflow resistance in steroid-induced OHT mouse eyes (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Netarsudil restored normal trabecular meshwork biomechanical properties in the steroid-induced ocular hypertension model after only 4 days of treatment.
source: We consider it noteworthy that NT appears to have restored normal TM biomechanical properties in our steroid-induced OHT model after only 4 days of treatment, and that this restoration was accompanied by significant morphological changes in the ECM of the TM.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: The rapid timescale of the observed extracellular matrix changes is consistent with observations from postmortem human eye preparations.
source: The rapid timescale of the observed ECM changes is consistent with observations from postmortem human eye preparations (Keller et al., 2009).
evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation to Keller et al., 2009.

claim: The time course of structural changes in the trabecular meshwork was consistent with the observed rapid (within 24 hr) pharmacodynamics of netarsudil on IOP.
source: The time course of structural changes in the TM was also consistent with the observed rapid (within 24 hr) pharmacodynamics of NT on IOP, significantly decreasing 1 and 3 months of OHT due to DEX treatment (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, respectively).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors inhibit monocyte differentiation in a murine model of ischemic/reperfusion cardiomyopathy.
source: Many mechanisms have been proposed for the systemically delivered anti-fibrotic effects of ROCKi, including inhibition of monocyte differentiation in a murine model of ischemic/reperfusion cardiomyopathy (Haudek et al., 2009), and macrophage infiltration of injured tissues in mouse models of multiple fibrotic diseases, including renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, diabetic nephropathy, renal allograft rejection, peritoneal fibrosis, and atherosclerosis (Wu et al., 2009; Knipe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haudek et al., 2009.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors inhibit macrophage infiltration of injured tissues in mouse models of multiple fibrotic diseases.
source: Many mechanisms have been proposed for the systemically delivered anti-fibrotic effects of ROCKi, including inhibition of monocyte differentiation in a murine model of ischemic/reperfusion cardiomyopathy (Haudek et al., 2009), and macrophage infiltration of injured tissues in mouse models of multiple fibrotic diseases, including renal tubulointerstitial fibrosis, diabetic nephropathy, renal allograft rejection, peritoneal fibrosis, and atherosclerosis (Wu et al., 2009; Knipe et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2009 and Knipe et al., 2015.

claim: Resident cells of the conventional outflow pathway primarily mediate netarsudil effects in view of the eye's immune-privileged status and local delivery.
source: In view of the eye's immune-privileged status and local delivery of NT in the present study, it seems likely that resident cells of the conventional outflow pathway primarily mediate NT effects.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the discussion based on the eye's immune-privileged status.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors inhibit TGF-β1-induced activation of p38 MAPK in other tissues.
source: In other tissues, RKIs inhibit TGF-β1-induced activation of p38 MAPK (Holvoet et al., 2017), activation of myocardin-related transcription factors (MRTFs), known to be master regulators of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Gasparics and Sebe, 2018), and reduced activation of NF-κB (Segain et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Holvoet et al., 2017.

claim: Myocardin-related transcription factors are known to be master regulators of epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
source: In other tissues, RKIs inhibit TGF-β1-induced activation of p38 MAPK (Holvoet et al., 2017), activation of myocardin-related transcription factors (MRTFs), known to be master regulators of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Gasparics and Sebe, 2018), and reduced activation of NF-κB (Segain et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gasparics and Sebe, 2018.

claim: Rho-kinase inhibitors reduce activation of NF-κB in other tissues.
source: In other tissues, RKIs inhibit TGF-β1-induced activation of p38 MAPK (Holvoet et al., 2017), activation of myocardin-related transcription factors (MRTFs), known to be master regulators of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (Gasparics and Sebe, 2018), and reduced activation of NF-κB (Segain et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Segain et al., 2003.

claim: Downstream targets of myocardin-related transcription factors include CTGF and YAP/TAZ.
source: Importantly, downstream targets of MRTFs include CTGF and YAP/TAZ, and TGF-β-mediated signaling through p38 and NF-κB (Raghunathan et al., 2013; Braunger et al., 2015; Inoue-Mochita et al., 2015; Tamm et al., 2015; Montecchi-Palmer et al., 2017; Hernandez et al., 2020), all of which participate in the regulation of TM contractility, mechanotransduction, and IOP homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: CTGF, YAP/TAZ, and TGF-β-mediated signaling through p38 and NF-κB participate in the regulation of trabecular meshwork contractility, mechanotransduction, and IOP homeostasis.
source: Importantly, downstream targets of MRTFs include CTGF and YAP/TAZ, and TGF-β-mediated signaling through p38 and NF-κB (Raghunathan et al., 2013; Braunger et al., 2015; Inoue-Mochita et al., 2015; Tamm et al., 2015; Montecchi-Palmer et al., 2017; Hernandez et al., 2020), all of which participate in the regulation of TM contractility, mechanotransduction, and IOP homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Atomic force microscopy measurements of stiffness reflect the stiffness of the extracellular matrix, not cells.
source: Thus, these measurements likely reflect the stiffness of the ECM, not cells (Wang et al., 2017b).
evidence: This interpretation is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017b.

claim: Before the approval of netarsudil in December 2017, four classes of glaucoma drugs were used to treat steroid-induced ocular hypertension.
source: Before the approval of NT in December 2017, four classes of glaucoma drugs (beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists, alpha-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and/or prostaglandin analogues) were used to treat steroid-induced OHT.
evidence: This is a statement of historical fact in the discussion.

claim: None of the four classes of glaucoma drugs used before netarsudil approval directly target tissues responsible for homeostatic regulation of IOP in healthy eyes.
source: Unfortunately, none of these drugs directly target tissues responsible for homeostatic regulation of IOP in healthy eyes nor for the dysregulation of IOP in steroid-induced glaucoma.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a limitation of previous treatments.

claim: Beta-adrenergic receptor antagonists, alpha-adrenergic agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, and prostaglandin analogues either decrease aqueous humor formation or divert aqueous humor from the conventional outflow pathway by increasing unconventional outflow drainage.
source: Instead, these drugs either decrease aqueous humor formation or divert aqueous humor from the conventional outflow pathway by increasing unconventional outflow drainage (Bucolo et al., 2015; Schmidl et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bucolo et al., 2015 and Schmidl et al., 2015.

claim: Prostaglandins are not often used to treat steroid-induced ocular hypertension due to concern about their effects on the blood-retinal barrier in vulnerable retinas.
source: Despite modest effects on conventional outflow (Brubaker et al., 2001; Wan et al., 2007; Bahler et al., 2008), prostaglandins are not often used to treat steroid-induced OHT due to concern about their effects on the blood-retinal barrier in vulnerable retinas (Table 1, Moroi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Netarsudil was the first agent to selectively target and modify conventional outflow morphology and function.
source: NT was the first agent to selectively target and modify conventional outflow morphology and function (Li et al., 2016; Ren et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016 and Ren et al., 2016.

claim: The current standard of care is for patients to be first treated with glaucoma medications that do not target the conventional outflow pathway, with netarsudil being used only when these drugs are ineffective at IOP lowering.
source: However, the current standard of care is for patients to be first treated with glaucoma medications that do not target the conventional outflow pathway, with NT being used only when these drugs are ineffective at IOP lowering.
evidence: This is a statement about current clinical practice in the discussion.

claim: 27 patients with steroid-induced ocular hypertension were treated with netarsudil in two independent patient populations.
source: In two independent patient populations, we found 27 patients that had steroid-induced OHT and were treated with NT.
evidence: This is a summary of the patient data in the discussion.

claim: Patients with steroid-induced ocular hypertension were first treated with a mean of 2.7 and 2.4 first- and second-line glaucoma medications.
source: Despite being first treated with multiple first- and second-line glaucoma medications (mean of 2.7 and 2.4), NT lowered IOP by an average of 7.9 mmHg in the first cohort and 6.0 mmHg in the second.
evidence: This is a summary of the patient data in the discussion.

claim: Netarsudil lowered IOP by an average of 7.9 mmHg in the first cohort and 6.0 mmHg in the second cohort of steroid-induced ocular hypertension patients.
source: Despite being first treated with multiple first- and second-line glaucoma medications (mean of 2.7 and 2.4), NT lowered IOP by an average of 7.9 mmHg in the first cohort and 6.0 mmHg in the second.
evidence: This is a summary of the patient data in the discussion.

claim: The trabecular meshwork is the location of pathology in steroid-induced ocular hypertension.
source: These observations are consistent with mechanistic data from our mouse model, supporting the concept that the TM is the location of pathology in steroid-induced OHT, and emphasizing the importance of targeting the conventional outflow pathway in this well-recognized condition.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the study findings.

claim: Steroid-induced ocular hypertension in mice was generated using nanotechnology, resulting in a model that closely matched steroid-induced observations in the human condition.
source: Steroid-induced OHT in mice was generated using nanotechnology (Agrahari et al., 2017), resulting in a model that closely matched steroid-induced observations in the human condition (decreased outflow facility, increased accumulation of ECM in the TM, and elevated IOP) (Johnson et al., 1990; Johnson and Knepper, 1994; Johnson et al., 1997; Clark et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mouse model of steroid-induced ocular hypertension closely matched human observations including decreased outflow facility, increased accumulation of extracellular matrix in the trabecular meshwork, and elevated IOP.
source: Steroid-induced OHT in mice was generated using nanotechnology (Agrahari et al., 2017), resulting in a model that closely matched steroid-induced observations in the human condition (decreased outflow facility, increased accumulation of ECM in the TM, and elevated IOP) (Johnson et al., 1990; Johnson and Knepper, 1994; Johnson et al., 1997; Clark et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a high incidence of ocular hypertension in patients receiving intravitreal glucocorticoid delivery implants to treat uveitis or macular edema.
source: The present study suggests the utility of our mouse model of steroid-induced OHT and its translational relevance to the human clinical condition, where there is a high incidence of OHT in patients receiving intravitreal GC delivery implants to treat uveitis or macular edema.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as context for the clinical relevance of the study.

claim: Human steroid-induced ocular hypertension patients who are refractory to standard glaucoma medications respond very well to netarsudil.
source: Our data indicate that human steroid-induced OHT patients who are refractory to standard glaucoma medications respond very well to NT.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the patient data.
